https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8g4.text: Image source, CBS News Image caption, An undated photo shows a car reportedly destroyed in an Iranian strike at Camp Buehring in Kuwait By Kayla Epstein and Bernd Debusmann Jr Published 16 September 2026, 16:23 BST Updated 2 hours ago Images showing widespread damage to multiple US sites in the Middle East from Iranian strikes have been obtained by the BBC's US partner CBS. The photos, provided by active military personnel, show a severed radar jet, flattened trailers and severely damaged buildings. The undated photos were taken at US bases and sites in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait. One member of the military, who was not named by CBS, said: "This is major damage to our bases that hasn't been communicated to the American public. "We're standing there with our eyes closed getting punched in the face." The White House referred the BBC to US Central Command. Centcom did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The photos, which have not been independently verified by the BBC, were published the day after a report from the Pentagon's watchdog confirmed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in the Middle East have been damaged and destroyed by Iran. One of the photos showed a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan Air Force Base in Saudi Arabia that has been ripped in half, its tail section crumpled into a tangled mess of metal. Image source, CBS News Image caption, An undated photo of a destroyed Boeing E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan air base in Saudi Arabia, about 62 miles (100km) south-east of the capital Riyadh While the photo is undated, BBC Verify previously confirmed a similar photo , apparently of the same radar aircraft in March. The Boeing E-3 Awacs are used to detect and track potential targets at long ranges to provide an early warning of possible threats. At the time, a US official told Reuters that 12 US personnel had been wounded, two of them seriously, in an Iranian attack on the air base. A pair of undated images reportedly from Camp Beuhring, Kuwait, show crumpled trailers, and a large tent-like structure that had been reduced to shreds as smoke billowed from the site. Image source, CBS News Image caption, Trailers destroyed by Iranian strike at Camp Buehring, Kuwait Image source, CBS News Image caption, Undated photo shows smoke billowing from a structure that sustained damage in an Iranian strike at Camp Buehring, Kuwait Another image shows a four-storey building damaged by an Iranian strike at Camp Arifjan, in Kuwait. Damage to the site was reported in March , including on satellite communications hardware, though it is not clear whether this image is from the same attack. Brian Katulis, a former national security official under both Democratic and Republican administrations, said that the damage visible in the images showed that "America had not adequately prepared its defences". "And there is strong evidence that US adversaries like China and Russia may have helped Iran in targeting," added Katulis, now a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute. "The Trump administration has done nothing to address these vulnerabilities." Image source, CBS News Image caption, Damage to a building can be seen in this photo from Camp Arifjan, Kuwait The images were published on the heels of a report from the Pentagon's watchdog, which found Iranian strikes had "damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman, and Jordan during the conflict". It also noted that equipment losses have totalled $3.7bn (Â£2.8bn). Overall, the US spent $33.4bn (Â£24.7bn) on the war up to 29 June, the report said. In the months after the war began, "dozens of US aircraft were destroyed or damaged", the report continues. The document lists several of the aircraft damaged, including five refuelling aircraft which were "damaged or destroyed on the ground in Saudi Arabia by Iranian munitions". A separate report , external from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) notes that the E-3 aircraft is no longer in production and would have to be replaced with a more modern equivalent, the E-7. The CBO noted that the E-3 aircraft alone costs $500m (Â£371m), and the estimated total cost of equipment lost in battle - including planes, drones and a terminal high altitude area defence system - amounts to $1.9b (Â£1.4b). CBO said that its review was subject to "uncertainty" because the defence department did not respond to its requests for information, requiring the agency to rely on government databases and public reports. Additionally, the extent of repairs and rebuilding that the US military plans to do remains unclear, according to the report. Brian Katulis of the Middle East Institute said that while "these costs show how the Trump administration burned through precious military resources without having much to show for it", the greater damage had been to broader US military readiness. "The United States had to divert military assets from Asia to the Middle East, leaving America and its partners in Asia more exposed and vulnerable to China," he said. "In addition, the depletion of US munitions makes Russia more willing to probe vulnerabilities with America's NATO allies and continue its aggressive war against Ukraine." While the US has the financial resources to address the equipment losses, it is already facing budgetary problems and may not be able to do so fast enough to prepare for potential flare-ups in the Middle East or elsewhere in the world, he added. Figure caption, Watch: What does the munitions shortage mean for the US? Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country. Since the war began Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel. On Tuesday night, the US House of Representatives voted for the third time to end the war in Iran, approving a measure that would force President Donald Trump to end US military action without congressional approval. The vote passed with the help of several Republicans, in what could be the final House vote on the matte r ahead of the US midterm elections in November. It faces an uncertain path to passage - the US Senate has not indicated if it will take up the matter. The same day, outgoing Republican Congressman Thomas Massie announced an attempt to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth as new details emerged about the Iran war's price tag for the US. The Trump administration backed Hegseth, with US attorney general Todd Blanche telling reporters he was "doing a phenomenal job". https://www.politico.eu/article/france-n.text: Leaders of France's far-right National Rally condemned Russia on Saturday in an unusual statement amid a rise in hybrid attacks and other provocations from Moscow. "We will never tolerate a foreign power, in this case, Russia, seeking to dictate, directly or indirectly, the policy of our country through intimidation, threats, destabilization or psychological pressure," party president Jordan Bardella and presidential candidate Marine Le Pen said in a joint statement . The remarks mention Russia's seizure of assets belonging to several companies still operating in the country, including French retailer Auchan and Swiss food and beverage giant Nestlé. The move, Bardella and Le Pen write, "is a hostile act against the interests of France and the nations of Europe" and "must be firmly condemned." Advertisement Advertisement But the statement also came after French President Emmanuel Macron chaired a rare crisis meeting Friday at which the country's political leaders, including Bardella, were briefed on the threats posed by Russia’s war in Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East. Le Pen and Bardella also cited the August drone attack at Leipzig airport , which German authorities attributed to Russia. "No provocation, clandestine operation, or destabilization effort could lead France to facilitate Russia’s achievement of its war aims in Ukraine," the far-right leaders write. The statement marks a rare show of unity within a party that has been divided over whether to treat the Kremlin as the enemy . Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 exposed fault lines within the movement. Le Pen has historically taken a warmer stance toward Russia; she has met Russian President Vladimir Putin in the past and her party took a €9.4 million loan from a Czech-Russian bank with links to the Kremlin, which has been repaid since. Bardella, a member of the European Parliament, has been more eager to portray Russia as a threat to France and Europe. Le Pen, who hopes to succeed Macron as president next year, is open to supplying military equipment to Ukraine but has ruled out providing additional financial assistance as Kyiv continues to fend off Russia's ongoing assault. "Firmness in the face of hostile actions and the pursuit of a diplomatic resolution to the war are not contradictory," reads the statement. The National Rally is expected to release its campaign platform before the end of the year, potentially clarifying its positions on Ukraine and Russia. Advertisement Advertisement

Photograph: NAZA/The Guardian NAZA ‘Tough to watch, impossible to ignore’: what the reviewers say about NAZA documentary Film interviewing military insiders about mass killing of civilians in Gaza receives widespread praise around the world Sammy Gecsoyler Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.42 EDT Last modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 11.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Critics around the world have hailed the award-winning documentary NAZA as a “brilliant and harrowing” film that is “impossible to ignore”. NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, was released in UK cinemas this week and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November. The investigative documentary, which contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders speaking anonymously on the rooftops of Tel Aviv at night, has received widespread praise. In a five-star review, the Financial Times’s Danny Leigh says that as a piece of cinema, “journalism and film-making brilliantly entwine”. The Times calls the film “hugely provocative and a disturbing account” of Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza, and the Irish Times brands NAZA an “essential record of engineered nightmare”. In a four-star review, the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw says the “ anguish of Gaza is brought into pin-sharp focus ”. British Vogue calls NAZA a “brilliant and harrowing film” that outlines the “restrained, meticulous, bone-chilling depiction of the progressive erasure of Gaza”. The magazine says the film “feels destined to become an enduring historical document, one which will and should be seen by generations to come”. Time Out magazine says NAZA “puts together a restrained, intelligent, articulate, precise and utterly damning case against Israel’s actions in Gaza and their ongoing actions through the region. As a work of cinema, it is exemplary. As a work of journalism, it is inarguable. As a document, it is an indictment.” The New York Times makes the film a “critic’s choice” and calls NAZA a “haunting” documentary that is “tough to watch, and impossible to ignore”. The Los Angeles Times says NAZA is a “stone-cold frightening” film that “burns the conscience”. And in New York magazine, it is described as “one of the most important films of our time”. The Hollywood Reporter praises NAZA as a “sober and thoroughly documented bombshell of an expose” that “leaves one with a deadening feeling, as if humanity may have lost all hope”. The Toronto Star says “NAZA is heartbreaking but essential viewing, questioning the systems that cause and quantify civilian death in modern warfare”. 44:17 NAZA: the film Israel does not want you to see - video The Spanish outlet El Mundo hailed NAZA as “the film of our time, a superb, electrifying, and devastating documentary about the systematic model of annihilation of the Palestinian people” that ultimately “points the finger at us. At night, in silence.” The French newspaper Le Monde says the film “has the effect of an uppercut that leaves the viewer stunned”, while the Danish culture magazine Soundvenue calls NAZA a “soul-crushing testimony to the genocide in Gaza” that is an “example of how the world increasingly seems like a dystopia”. The United Arab Emirates’ state-owned newspaper the National calls NAZA a “sickeningly tough film to watch”, and an editorial in the Israeli-outlet Haaretz says the film is “trying to force Israelis to confront what they already know: that Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza has left a black stain”. When the film opened in Italy last month, it topped the charts . The Italian newspaper Corriere della Sera says NAZA lasts “only 80 minutes, but no more is needed: the ‘scientific’ coldness with which the interviewees reconstruct how they are destroying Gaza is something unforgettable”. 1:55 NAZA - official trailer The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during the Gaza war, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die. Various bodies, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was received a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went on to win the special jury prize .
